diplodocus:enwiki:7.title: Diplodocus (Second Dinosaur Rush and Diplodocus carnegii)

diplodocus:eswiki:9.title: Diplodocus (Coloración y estructura de la piel)

facts.statement: The genus Diplodocus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1878

facts.statement: The first Diplodocus fossils were discovered in 1877 by S. W. Williston.
facts.quote: The first fossils of Diplodocus were discovered in 1877 by S. W. Williston.

facts.statement: Modern mass estimates for Diplodocus carnegii typically range from 12 to 14.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: Modern mass estimates for D. carnegii have tended to be in the 12 - 14.8 MT range.

facts.statement: Diplodocus possessed small, peg-like teeth that pointed forward and were located only in the front sections of its jaws.
facts.quote: Diplodocus had small, 'peg'-like teeth that pointed forward and were only present in the anterior sections of the jaws.

facts.statement: Diplodocus had a small braincase and a neck made of at least 15 vertebrae.
facts.quote: Its braincase was small, and the neck was composed of at least 15 vertebrae.

facts.statement: The tail of Diplodocus makes up approximately 55% of its total body length.
facts.quote: The estimated tail length of Diplodocus makes up approximately 55% of the total body length

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that the Diplodocus tail may have served a defensive, noisemaking, or tactile function.
facts.quote: Some speculation exists as to whether it may have had a defensive or noisemaking (by cracking it like a coachwhip) or, as more recently suggested, tactile function.

facts.statement: The middle part of the Diplodocus tail featured oddly shaped chevron bones known as "double beams," which gave the genus its name.
facts.quote: The middle part of the tail had "double beams" (oddly shaped chevron bones on the underside, which gave Diplodocus its name).

facts.statement: Diplodocus lacked claws on all front limbs except one digit, which had an unusually large, flattened claw detached from the hand bones.
facts.quote: Diplodocus lacked claws on all but one digit of the front limb, and this claw was unusually large relative to other sauropods, flattened from side to side, and detached from the bones of the hand.

facts.statement: Skin impressions discovered in 1990 revealed that some Diplodocus species had narrow, pointed keratinous spines similar to those of an iguana.
facts.quote: The discovery of partial diplodocid skin impressions in 1990 showed that some species had narrow, pointed, keratinous spines, much like those on an iguana.

facts.statement: In 2025, researchers identified probable melanosomes indicating diverse colors in the scales of juvenile Diplodocus specimens.
facts.quote: In 2025, Gallagher et al. identified probable melanosomes representing diverse colours based on microbodies found within epidermis in the scales of juvenile specimens of Diplodocus sp. from the same quarry

facts.statement: The type species of Diplodocus is Diplodocus longus, which is considered a nomen dubium.
facts.quote: type_species: Diplodocus longus (nomen dubium)

facts.statement: Diplodocus includes the species D. carnegii (named by Hatcher in 1901) and D. hallorum (named by Gillette in 1991, originally classified as Seismosaurus).
facts.quote: subdivision: D. carnegii Hatcher, 1901 D. hallorum (Gillette, 1991) (originally Seismosaurus)

facts.statement: Seismosaurus is a synonym of Diplodocus, a name established by Gillette in 1991.
facts.quote: synonyms: Seismosaurus Gillette, 1991

facts.statement: Remains of predators Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus found in the same strata suggest they coexisted with Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Its great size may have been a deterrent to the predators Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus: their remains have been found in the same strata, which suggests that they coexisted with Diplodocus.

facts.statement: The first Diplodocus fossils were collected in 1877 at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado, by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Wendell Williston.
facts.quote: The first record of Diplodocus comes from Marshall P. Felch's quarry at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado, when several fossils were collected by Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Wendell Williston in 1877.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh named the first specimen Diplodocus longus in 1878.
facts.quote: The specimen was sent to the Yale Peabody Museum and was named Diplodocus longus ('long double-beam') by paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878.

facts.statement: Diplodocus was named during the Bone Wars, a competition between Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope.
facts.quote: Marsh named Diplodocus during the Bone Wars, his competition with Philadelphian paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope to collect and describe as many fossil taxa as possible.

facts.statement: The first complete diplodocid skull was collected in 1883 and consisted of an articulated skull, mandibles, and partial atlas.
facts.quote: One specimen (USNM V 2672), an articulated complete skull, mandibles, and partial atlas was collected in 1883, and was the first complete diplodocid skull to be reported.

facts.statement: In 1897, the American Museum of Natural History found a Diplodocus skeleton at Como Bluff.
facts.quote: The American Museum of Natural History was the first to launch an expedition, finding a semi-articulated partial postcranial skeleton containing many vertebrae of Diplodocus in at Como Bluff in 1897.

facts.statement: A massive and well-preserved Diplodocus skeleton was discovered in 1899 in Sheep Creek, Wyoming, on an expedition funded by Andrew Carnegie.
facts.quote: The most notable Diplodocus find also came in 1899 on an expedition funded by Scottish-American steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie, when crew members from the Carnegie Museum of Natural History discovered a massive and well preserved skeleton of Diplodocus in the Morrison Formation of Sheep Creek, Wyoming.

facts.statement: The London cast of Diplodocus was the first sauropod mount displayed outside the United States and was requested by King Edward VII.
facts.quote: The London cast specifically became very popular; its casting was requested by King Edward VII and it was the first sauropod mount put on display outside of the United States.

facts.statement: In 1909, Earl Douglass discovered Diplodocus fossils at Dinosaur National Monument, located on the border of Colorado and Utah.
facts.quote: The Carnegie Museum of Natural History made another landmark discovery in 1909 when Earl Douglass unearthed several caudal vertebrae from Apatosaurus in what is now Dinosaur National Monument on the border region between Colorado and Utah, with the sandstone dating to the Kimmeridgian of the Morrison Formation.

facts.statement: Between 1909 and 1922, excavations at Dinosaur National Monument uncovered over 120 dinosaur individuals and more than 1,600 bones.
facts.quote: From 1909 to 1922, with the Carnegie Museum excavating the quarry, eventually unearthing over 120 dinosaur individuals and 1,600+ bones, many of the associated skeletons being very complete and are on display in several American museums.

facts.statement: Earl Douglass found a semi-articulated diplodocine skull with mandibles at Dinosaur National Monument in 1912.
facts.quote: In 1912, Douglass found a semi articulated skull of a diplodocine with mandibles (CM 11161) in the Monument.

facts.statement: A nearly complete juvenile Diplodocus skull was collected in 1921, representing the first known juvenile skull of the genus.
facts.quote: A nearly complete skull of a juvenile Diplodocus was collected by Douglass in 1921, and it is the first known from a Diplodocus.

facts.statement: The National Museum of Natural History collected a Diplodocus skeleton at the Carnegie Quarry in 1923.
facts.quote: Another Diplodocus skeleton was collected at the Carnegie Quarry in Dinosaur National Monument, Utah, by the National Museum of Natural History in 1923.

facts.statement: The USNM V 10865 skeleton is one of the most complete Diplodocus specimens, featuring a well-preserved dorsal column.
facts.quote: The skeleton (USNM V 10865) is one of the most complete known from Diplodocus, consisting of a semi-articulated partial postcranial skeleton, including a well preserved dorsal column.

facts.statement: In 1979, hikers discovered Diplodocus vertebrae near petroglyphs in a canyon west of San Ysidro, New Mexico.
facts.quote: Few Diplodocus finds came for many years until 1979, when three hikers came across several vertebrae stuck in elevated stone next to several petroglyphs in a canyon west of San Ysidro, New Mexico.

facts.statement: An expedition led by David D. Gillette collected a Diplodocus specimen between 1985 and 1990 after it was reported to the New Mexican Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: The find was reported to the New Mexican Museum of Natural History, who dispatched an expedition led by David D. Gillette in 1985, that collected the specimen after several visits from 1985 to 1990.

facts.statement: A Diplodocus specimen (NMMNH P-3690) found in New Mexico was preserved with 230 gastroliths, vertebrae, a partial pelvis, and a right femur.
facts.quote: The specimen was preserved in semi-articulation, including 230 gastroliths, with several vertebrae, partial pelvis, and right femur and was prepared and deposited at the New Mexican Museum of Natural History under NMMNH P-3690.

facts.statement: David D. Gillette named a New Mexico Diplodocus specimen Seismosaurus hallorum in 1991, later amending the name in 1994.
facts.quote: The specimen was not described until 1991 in the Journal of Paleontology, where Gillette named it Seismosaurus halli (Jim and Ruth Hall's seismic lizard), though in 1994, Gillette published an amendment changing the name to S. hallorum.

facts.statement: The Museum of the Rockies discovered the Mother's Day Quarry in Montana in 1994, which was later excavated by other institutions.
facts.quote: In 1994, the Museum of the Rockies discovered a very productive fossil site at Mother's Day Quarry in Carbon County, Montana from the Salt Wash member of the Morrison Formation that was later excavated by the Cincinnati Museum of Natural History and Science in 1996, and after that the Bighorn Basin Paleontological Institute in 2017.

facts.statement: The Mother's Day Quarry in Montana yielded many isolated Diplodocus bones ranging from juveniles to adults in pristine condition.
facts.quote: The quarry was very productive, having mostly isolated Diplodocus bones from juveniles to adults in pristine preservation.

facts.statement: Fossils from the Mother's Day Quarry include frequent skin impressions, pathologies, and articulated Diplodocus specimens.
facts.quote: The quarry notably had a great disparity between the amount of juveniles and adults in the quarry, as well as the frequent preservation of skin impressions, pathologies, and some articulated specimens from Diplodocus.

facts.statement: A nearly complete juvenile Diplodocus skull found at the Mother's Day Quarry provides rare evidence of dietary changes during growth.
facts.quote: One specimen, a nearly complete skull of a juvenile Diplodocus, was found at the quarry and is one of few known and highlighted ontogenetic dietary changes in the genus.

facts.statement: Two partial Diplodocus skeletons (SHN 177 and 178) were discovered in the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal.
facts.quote: In the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal, two partial skeletons SHN 177 and 178 were discovered and regarded as representing the same taxon.

facts.statement: Diagnostic Diplodocus remains were found in 2026 in the Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Spain without a specific species assignment.
facts.quote: In 2026, diagnostic remains of Diplodocus were found in the Upper Jurassic Villar del Arzobispo Formation of Spain, but not assigned to any particular species.

facts.statement: Diplodocus is the type genus and namesake of the family Diplodocidae.
facts.quote: Diplodocus is both the type genus of, and gives its name to, the Diplodocidae, the family in which it belongs.

facts.statement: Diplodocids are characterized by long necks and tails, a horizontal posture, and forelimbs shorter than hind limbs.
facts.quote: All are characterized by long necks and tails and a horizontal posture, with forelimbs shorter than hind limbs.

facts.statement: The subfamily Diplodocinae includes Diplodocus and its closest relatives, such as Barosaurus.
facts.quote: A subfamily, the Diplodocinae, was erected to include Diplodocus and its closest relatives, including Barosaurus.

facts.statement: Apatosaurus is a diplodocid but belongs to the sister subfamily Apatosaurinae, not Diplodocinae.
facts.quote: More distantly related is the contemporaneous Apatosaurus, which is still considered a diplodocid, although not a diplodocine, as it is a member of the sister subfamily Apatosaurinae.

facts.statement: Some authors identify the Portuguese Dinheirosaurus and African Tornieria as close relatives of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The Portuguese Dinheirosaurus and the African Tornieria have also been identified as close relatives of Diplodocus by some authors.

facts.statement: The clade Diplodocoidea includes diplodocids, dicraeosaurids, rebbachisaurids, Suuwassea, Amphicoelias, possibly Haplocanthosaurus, and/or nemegtosaurids.
facts.quote: Diplodocoidea comprises the diplodocids, as well as the dicraeosaurids, rebbachisaurids, Suuwassea, Amphicoelias possibly Haplocanthosaurus, and/or the nemegtosaurids.

facts.statement: Diplodocoidea is the sister group to Macronaria, which includes camarasaurids, brachiosaurids, and titanosaurians.
facts.quote: The clade is the sister group to Macronaria (camarasaurids, brachiosaurids and titanosaurians).

facts.statement: Diplodocus carnegii, named after Andrew Carnegie, is best known from the near-complete skeleton 'Dippy' (CM 84) collected by Jacob Wortman and named by John Bell Hatcher in 1901.
facts.quote: Diplodocus carnegii (also spelled incorrectly D. carnegiei), named after Andrew Carnegie, is the best known, mainly due to a near-complete skeleton known as Dippy (specimen CM 84) collected by Jacob Wortman, of the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and described and named by John Bell Hatcher in 1901.

facts.statement: Diplodocus hallorum was first described in 1991 by Gillette as Seismosaurus halli from a partial skeleton including vertebrae, pelvis, and ribs.
facts.quote: Diplodocus hallorum, first described in 1991 by Gillette as Seismosaurus halli from a partial skeleton comprising vertebrae, pelvis and ribs (specimen NMMNH P-3690).

facts.statement: In 2004, a presentation argued that Seismosaurus was a junior synonym of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: In 2004, a presentation at the annual conference of the Geological Society of America made a case for Seismosaurus being a junior synonym of Diplodocus.

facts.statement: A 2006 publication renamed Seismosaurus to Diplodocus hallorum and speculated it might be the same species as D. longus.
facts.quote: This was followed by a much more detailed publication in 2006, which not only renamed the species Diplodocus hallorum, but also speculated that it could prove to be the same as D. longus.

facts.statement: A 2015 analysis suggested that opinions linking D. hallorum and D. longus were based on more complete referred specimens of D. longus.
facts.quote: A 2015 analysis of diplodocid relationships noted that these opinions are based on the more complete referred specimens of Diplodocus longus.

facts.statement: Detailed analysis suggests the original fossil of D. longus lacks features necessary to compare with other specimens.
facts.quote: Though several more complete specimens have been attributed to D. longus, detailed analysis has suggested that the original fossil lacks the necessary features to allow comparison with other specimens.

facts.statement: A petition to the ICZN proposed making D. carnegii the new type species of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: A petition to the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN) was being considered, which proposed to make D. carnegii the new type species.

facts.statement: The ICZN rejected the proposal to change the type species, maintaining D. longus as the type species of Diplodocus.
facts.quote: The proposal was rejected by the ICZN and D. longus has been maintained as the type species.

facts.statement: Marsh named Diplodocus lacustris in 1884 based on a snout with slender teeth from Morrison, Colorado.
facts.quote: Diplodocus lacustris was named by Marsh in 1884 based on a snout with comparatively slender teeth (YPM 1922) from Morrison, Colorado.

facts.statement: In 2015, Tschopp and colleagues argued that the snout of the D. lacustris specimen belonged to Camarasaurus and the teeth could not be identified to a genus.
facts.quote: In 2015, Tschopp and colleagues argued that the snout of the specimen actually belonged to Camarasaurus, and that the teeth cannot be identified to a particular genus.

facts.statement: William Jacob Holland named Diplodocus hayi in 1924 based on a braincase and partial skeleton found near Sheridan, Wyoming.
facts.quote: Diplodocus hayi was named by William Jacob Holland in 1924 based on a braincase and partial postcranial skeleton (HMNS 175), including a nearly complete vertebral column, found in the Morrison Formation strata near Sheridan, Wyoming.

facts.statement: In 2015, Tschopp and colleagues reassessed D. hayi as its own genus, Galeamopus.
facts.quote: D. hayi remained a species of Diplodocus until reassessment by Emmanuel Tschopp and colleagues determined that it was its own genus, Galeamopus, in 2015.

facts.statement: Diplodocus is one of the best-studied dinosaurs due to a wealth of skeletal remains.
facts.quote: Due to a wealth of skeletal remains, Diplodocus is one of the best-studied dinosaurs.

facts.statement: A 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates sauropods likely could not breathe through nostrils while submerged due to water pressure.
facts.quote: A 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates that sauropods probably could not have breathed through their nostrils when the rest of the body was submerged, as the water pressure on the chest wall would be too great.

facts.statement: Reconstructions show great pneumaticity in the neck and thorax of Diplodocus, which could have aided respiration like in birds.
facts.quote: Reconstructions of the neck and thorax of Diplodocus show great pneumaticity, which could have played a role in respiration as it does in birds.

facts.statement: A 1910 reconstruction by Oliver P. Hay depicted Diplodocus with splayed, lizard-like limbs.
facts.quote: a classic 1910 reconstruction by Oliver P. Hay depicts two Diplodocus with splayed lizard-like limbs on the banks of a river.

facts.statement: Sauropod footprints found in the 1930s disproved the theory that Diplodocus had a sprawling, lizard-like gait.
facts.quote: Finds of sauropod footprints in the 1930s eventually put Hay's theory to rest.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that Diplodocus held its neck at a high angle is contradicted by evidence that the inner ear alignment suggests a horizontal neck pose.
facts.quote: However, this idea might be contradicted due to the inner ear of diplodocoids actually being in alignment for a horizontal neck pose.

facts.statement: A 1992 study indicated that the longest-necked diplodocids would have required a heart weighing 1.6 tons, which is one-tenth of their body weight.
facts.quote: A 1992 Columbia University study of diplodocid neck structure indicated that the longest necks would have required a 1.6-ton heart – a tenth of the animal's body weight.

facts.statement: Diplodocines possessed highly unusual teeth with long, slender crowns that were elliptical in cross-section and ended in a blunt, triangular point.
facts.quote: Diplodocines have highly unusual teeth compared to other sauropods. The crowns are long and slender, and elliptical in cross-section, while the apex forms a blunt, triangular point.

facts.statement: Up to five replacement teeth were developing within each tooth socket of Diplodocus at any given time.
facts.quote: Within each tooth socket, as many as five replacement teeth were developing to replace the next one.

facts.statement: Despite debates on neck flexibility, Diplodocus could browse vegetation from low levels up to about 4 meters while on all fours.
facts.quote: The flexibility of Diplodocus neck is debated but it should have been able to browse from low levels to about 4 m when on all fours.

facts.statement: Diplodocus could rear up into a stable tripodal posture using its tail as a prop, potentially increasing its feeding height to about 11 meters.
facts.quote: It also had the advantage of using its large tail as a 'prop' which would allow for a very stable tripodal posture. In a tripodal posture Diplodocus could potentially increase its feeding height up to about 11 m.

facts.statement: The relative lengths of Diplodocus's front and hind limbs support the hypothesis that it fed from submerged water plants or riverbanks.
facts.quote: This concept of the feeding posture is supported by the relative lengths of front and hind limbs.

facts.statement: Matthew Cobley et al. (2013) disputed the idea that Diplodocus could feed from submerged plants, arguing that large muscles and cartilage limited neck movement.
facts.quote: Matthew Cobley et al. (2013) disputed this, finding that large muscles and cartilage would have limited neck movements.

facts.statement: Mike Taylor disputed Cobley et al.'s conclusions in 2013 and 2014, arguing that Diplodocus neck flexibility was greater than bone structure alone suggested.
facts.quote: The conclusions of Cobley et al. were disputed in 2013 and 2014 by Mike Taylor, who analyzed the amount and positioning of intervertebral cartilage to determine the flexibility of the neck of Diplodocus and Apatosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2010 study described a juvenile Diplodocus skull with a non-blunt snout and teeth not confined to the front, suggesting different feeding behaviors between juveniles and adults.
facts.quote: In 2010, Whitlock et al. described a juvenile skull at the time referred to Diplodocus (CM 11255) that differed greatly from adult skulls of the same genus: its snout was not blunt, and the teeth were not confined to the front of the snout.

facts.statement: Dental microwear patterns suggest Diplodocus partitioned resources with Camarasaurus by eating softer foods.
facts.quote: Dental microwear patterns of Diplodocus suggest that it partitioned its resources with Camarasaurus; the former ate softer foods than the latter.

facts.statement: Similar microwear patterns between juvenile Camarasaurus and adult Diplodocus suggest that adults may have competed with juveniles of the other species for food.
facts.quote: However, juvenile Camarasaurus had similar microwear to adult Diplodocus, suggesting that adult Diplodocus may have competed with juvenile Camarasaurus for food.

facts.statement: Researchers once hypothesized that the oversized neck of Diplodocus was primarily for sexual display rather than feeding.
facts.quote: it was also suggested that the oversized neck of Diplodocus and its relatives may have been primarily a sexual display, with any other feeding benefits coming second

facts.statement: A 2011 study refuted the hypothesis that Diplodocus used its neck primarily for sexual display.
facts.quote: A 2011 study refuted this idea in detail

facts.statement: Diplodocus laid surprisingly small eggs and clutches for an animal of its massive size.
facts.quote: For Diplodocus and other sauropods, the size of clutches and individual eggs were surprisingly small for such large animals

facts.statement: The small size of Diplodocus eggs is thought to be an adaptation to avoid predation risks associated with long incubation times.
facts.quote: This appears to have been an adaptation to predation pressures, as large eggs would require greater incubation time and thus would be at greater risk

facts.statement: Early 2000s bone histology studies suggested Diplodocus grew very fast and reached sexual maturity in just over a decade.
facts.quote: Based on bone histology studies in the early 2000s, it was suggested that Diplodocus and other sauropods grew at a very fast rate, reaching sexual maturity at just over a decade

facts.statement: The Morrison Formation, where Diplodocus fossils are found, dates from 156.3 to 146.8 million years ago.
facts.quote: The Morrison Formation is a sequence of shallow marine and alluvial sediments which, according to radiometric dating, ranges between 156.3 million years old (Ma) at its base, and 146.8 million years old at the top

facts.statement: The Morrison Formation environment where Diplodocus lived was semi-arid with distinct wet and dry seasons.
facts.quote: This formation is interpreted as a semi-arid environment with distinct wet and dry seasons

facts.statement: The Morrison Basin, the habitat of Diplodocus, stretched from New Mexico to Alberta and Saskatchewan.
facts.quote: The Morrison Basin, where many dinosaurs lived, stretched from New Mexico to Alberta and Saskatchewan

facts.statement: Diplodocus shared its environment with ray-finned fishes, frogs, salamanders, turtles, lizards, crocodylomorphs, and pterosaurs.
facts.quote: Other vertebrates that shared the same paleoenvironment included ray-finned fishes, frogs, salamanders, turtles like Dorsetochelys, sphenodonts, lizards, terrestrial and aquatic crocodylomorphs such as Hoplosuchus, and several species of pterosaur like Harpactognathus and Mesadactylus

facts.statement: Allosaurus was the top predator in the Morrison food web, accounting for 70 to 75% of theropod specimens.
facts.quote: Allosaurus accounted for 70 to 75% of theropod specimens and was at the top trophic level of the Morrison food web

facts.statement: Diplodocus lived in what is now western North America during the Late Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Vivió en lo que es hoy el oeste de Norteamérica durante el período Jurásico Superior

facts.statement: Diplodocus is easily identifiable by its classic shape, long neck and tail, and four robust legs.
facts.quote: El Diplodocus está entre los dinosaurios más fácilmente identificables, con su forma clásica, cuello y cola largos, y cuatro patas robustas

facts.statement: For many years, Diplodocus was considered the largest known dinosaur.
facts.quote: Durante muchos años, era el dinosaurio más grande conocido

facts.statement: The name Diplodocus is derived from Greek words meaning 'double' and 'beam', referring to the chevron-shaped bones along the underside of the tail.
facts.quote: El nombre genérico Diplodocus es la forma en neolatín derivada del griego διπλόος (diploös) «doble» y δοκός (dokos) «viga», en referencia a la forma de los huesos en chevrón a lo largo de la parte inferior de la cola

facts.statement: The term Diplodocus was coined by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878.
facts.quote: El término fue cuñado por Othniel Charles Marsh en 1878

facts.statement: The genus Diplodocus was described by Marsh in 1878.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1878

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Diplodocus is Diplodocus carnegii.
facts.quote: type_species: Diplodocus carnegii

facts.statement: Diplodocus longus and Diplodocus hallorum are recognized subdivisions within the genus Diplodocus.
facts.quote: subdivision: * Diplodocus longus Marsh, 1887 (Dudosa) Diplodocus hallorum (Gillette, 1991) Lucas et al., 2004

facts.statement: Seismosaurus is a synonym of the genus Diplodocus.
facts.quote: synonyms: * Seismosaurus Gillette, 1991

facts.statement: Diplodocus is the most frequently depicted sauropod dinosaur, displayed in more locations than any other.
facts.quote: Diplodocus has been a frequently depicted dinosaur, being on display within more places than any other sauropod dinosaur

facts.statement: Andrew Carnegie donated many mounted casts of Diplodocus, known as 'Dippy', to world leaders in the early 20th century, familiarizing the public with the dinosaur.
facts.quote: The donation of many mounted skeletal casts of "Dippy" by industrialist Andrew Carnegie to potentates around the world at the beginning of the 20th century did much to familiarize it to people worldwide

facts.statement: A World War I landship named the Boirault machine was nicknamed 'Diplodocus militaris' due to its impractical design.
facts.quote: A war machine (landship) from World War I named Boirault machine was designed in 1915, later deemed impractical and hence given the nickname "Diplodocus militaris"

facts.statement: Diplodocus is considered one of the best-known dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Los Diplodocus están entre los dinosaurios mejor conocidos.

facts.statement: Diplodocus were very large quadrupeds with long necks and extensive whip-like tails.
facts.quote: Fueron animales cuadrúpedos muy grandes, de cuello largo y con una extensa cola en forma de látigo.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Diplodocus carnegii, CM 84, is the most complete known, estimated at 25 meters long and 6.5 meters tall at the neck.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo de Diplodocus carnegii, CM 84 es el más completo hallado de su género, estimado en alrededor de 25 metros de largo y 6.5 m de alto al cuello.

facts.statement: When described in 1991, David Gillette estimated Diplodocus hallorum could have reached 52 meters in length, making it the longest known dinosaur at the time.
facts.quote: Cuando fue descrito en 1991, el descubridor, David Gillete, calculó que pudo haber medido hasta 52 metros de largo, haciéndole el dinosaurio más largo conocido, excepto los dudosos dinosaurios pobremente conocidos como Amphicoelias.

facts.statement: Recent revisions showed that the giant tail vertebrae were located further back in the tail than originally placed by Gillette.
facts.quote: Una revisión más reciente demuestra que las vértebras gigantes de la cola estaban colocadas realmente más adelante en la cola que lo que D. Gillete las había ubicado originalmente.

facts.statement: The middle part of the tail had 'double beams', strange chevron-shaped bones that give Diplodocus its name.
facts.quote: La parte media de la cola tenía "dobles vigas", huesos cheurones de forma extraña que le dan a los Diplodocus su nombre.

facts.statement: Speculations suggest Diplodocus may have used their tails for defense or to make noise like a whip.
facts.quote: Existen especulaciones acerca de que los diplódocos podrían haber utilizado su cola como defensa o para hacer ruido como un látigo.

facts.statement: The tail may also have served as a counterbalance for the neck.
facts.quote: También podría haber servido como contrapeso para el cuello.

facts.statement: In 2025, a study analyzed fossilized scales attributed to a juvenile Diplodocus from the Mother's Day Quarry in Montana, USA.
facts.quote: En 2025 se publicó un estudio que analizó escamas fosilizadas atribuidas a un ejemplar juvenil de Diplodocus procedente del yacimiento Mother's Day Quarry (Montana, Estados Unidos).

facts.statement: Analysis revealed two distinct types of melanosomes: one elongated and one disc-shaped.
facts.quote: El análisis reveló la presencia de dos tipos distintos de melanosomas: uno alargado y otro de forma discoidal.

facts.statement: Based on the shape and size of melanosomes, authors propose the skin had predominantly dark tones, such as brown or black.
facts.quote: Según la forma y tamaño de estos melanosomas, los autores proponen que la piel presentaba tonalidades predominantemente oscuras, como marrones o negros.

facts.statement: Since the 1970s, the general consensus considers sauropods as firmly terrestrial animals, browsing among trees, ferns, and shrubs.
facts.quote: Desde la década de 1970, el consenso general tiene los saurópodos como animales firmemente terrestres, navegando entre árboles, helechos y arbustos.

facts.statement: Comparisons between scleral rings of diplodocines and modern birds and reptiles suggest they may have been catemeral, active throughout the day in short intervals.
facts.quote: Las comparaciones entre los anillos esclerales de diplodócinos y las aves y reptiles modernos sugieren que pueden haber sido catemeral, activos a lo largo del día a intervalos cortos.

facts.statement: Marsh and later Hatcher hypothesized the animal was aquatic due to the position of its nasal openings at the apex of the skull.
facts.quote: Marsh y luego Hatcher supusieron que el animal era acuático, debido a la posición de sus aberturas nasales en el ápice del cráneo.

facts.statement: A 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates sauropods probably could not breathe through their nose when the rest of the body was submerged, as water pressure on the thoracic wall would be too great.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 1951 de Kenneth A. Kermack indica que los saurópodos probablemente no podrían haber respirado por la nariz cuando el resto del cuerpo estaba sumergido, ya que la presión del agua en la pared del tórax sería demasiado grande.

facts.statement: They probably had an avian respiratory system, which is more efficient than that of mammals and reptiles.
facts.quote: Probablemente tenían un sistema respiratorio aviar, que es más eficiente que un sistema de mamíferos y reptiles.

facts.statement: Diplodocus possessed long, thin, elliptical tooth crowns with a blunt, triangular tip.
facts.quote: Las coronas dentales eran largas, delgadas y elípticas en sección transversal, mientras que el ápice forma un punto romo y triangular.

facts.statement: Diplodocus and other diplodocids had a radically different feeding mechanism compared to other sauropods.
facts.quote: Esto significa que los Diplodocus y otros diplodócidos tenían un mecanismo de alimentación radicalmente diferente al de otros saurópodos.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Diplodocus likely fed by stripping branches using one side of its snout.
facts.quote: El deshojamiento de ramas usando un lado del hocico es la forma de alimentación más probable del Diplodocus

facts.statement: Diplodocus could strip longer sections of stems in a single action due to its elongated preorbital skull region.
facts.quote: Gracias a que contaba con una alongada región preorbital del cráneo (delante de los ojos), podría deshojar porciones más largas de tallos en una sola acción.

facts.statement: Some scientists speculate that Diplodocus grazed on submerged aquatic plants because its head could reach below body level.

facts.statement: In 2013, Cobley and colleagues disputed previous ideas, arguing that large muscles and cartilage would limit Diplodocus neck movement.

facts.statement: Young and colleagues used biomechanical models in 2012 to examine Diplodocus skull performance.
facts.quote: Young y colegas en 2012 utilizaron modelos biomecánicos para examinar el rendimiento del cráneo de Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Michael D'Emic and colleagues discovered that Diplodocus teeth were replaced continuously, usually in less than 35 days.
facts.quote: Los dientes también fueron reemplazados continuamente a lo largo de sus vidas, por lo general en menos de 35 días, como fue descubierto por Michael D'Emic y colegas.

facts.statement: Up to five replacement teeth developed within each tooth socket to replace the next one.
facts.quote: Dentro de cada alveolo dentario, se desarrollaron hasta cinco dientes de reemplazo para reemplazar el siguiente.

facts.statement: Whitlock and colleagues described a juvenile Diplodocus skull (CM 11255) in 2010 that differed significantly from adult skulls of the same genus.

facts.statement: Differences between the juvenile and adult skulls suggest that adults and juveniles fed differently.
facts.quote: Estas diferencias sugieren que los adultos y los juveniles se alimentaban de manera diferente.

facts.statement: The distribution of gastroliths found with a D. hallorum fossil suggests these animals may have had a digestive system similar to modern birds, with a crop and gizzard.
